authoring.value:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x)$ whose ordinary integral exists over the interval, the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .
$$

Notice that $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function, we have

$$
\int_{-2}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx = 2 \int_{0}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx.
$$

The displayed example integrands are continuous on their intervals. If an integrand has an internal singularity, first check the convergence of every one-sided improper integral; symmetry cannot cancel independently divergent integrals. A Cauchy principal value requires an explicit principal-value convention.
authoring.rationale: The actual example integrands are continuous, but the universal symmetry rule must require existence of the ordinary integral. Qualify the rule and explicitly distinguish ordinary improper convergence from principal-value regularization. Original source prompt, answer fields, and historical original solution remain preserved.
